## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Ambapālītherīgāthā* (Thig 13.1) is one of the most celebrated poems in the *Therīgāthā* of the Pali Canon [Crosby 2014]. In these verses, the courtesan-turned-nun Ambapālī reflects upon impermanence (*anicca*) by contrasting the beauty of her youthful body with its physical deterioration in old age [Crosby 2014]. Moving methodically through various parts of her body—such as her hair, once fragrant and black like the down of bees but now resembling hemp or bark, and her feet, once soft but now cracked and wrinkled—she concludes each stanza with the recurring refrain affirming the truth of the Buddha's teaching: "Such and not otherwise runneth the rune, the word of the Soothsayer" [Crosby, Theravada Buddhism; Crosby 2014]. Scholars note that while male monastics typically contemplated external corpses for *asubha* (foulness) meditation, Ambapālī provides a clear canonical instance of a woman meditating upon her own aging physical form [Crosby 2014]. Canonical tradition treats her background as a courtesan without moral condemnation, reflecting an autonomy that enabled her to sponsor the Sangha independently [Crosby 2014].
In Pali exegetical literature, DharmaNexus notes 37 matching passages between the poem and the *Therīgāthā-aṭṭhakathā*, where almost the entire text (§0.3–20.1) is embedded and explained [DharmaNexus]. In addition, DharmaNexus calculates cross-language alignments with various Buddhist texts, sharing passages with works preserved in Tibetan such as Haribhaṭṭa's *Jātakamālā* (D4152), the *Śraddhotpādapradīpa* (D4195), Kṣemendra's *Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā* (D4155-2), and the *Ratnākarasūtra* (D0124), as well as the Chinese *Qishi yinben jing* (T 25) [DharmaNexus].
